subject: history
title: Elizabeth I: Settlement, Mary Stuart and the Armada
welcome_lead: From the 1559 Settlement to the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588.
meta_desc: AQA A-Level adventure on Elizabeth I: Religious Settlement 1559, execution of Mary Queen of Scots 1587 and the Armada 1588.
final_note: You can evaluate Elizabethan stability and the threats it survived.

concepts.def: Acts of Supremacy (Elizabeth as Supreme Governor) and Uniformity establishing a moderate Protestant national church.
Statute reimposing the Book of Common Prayer (a hybrid of 1549/1552) and mandating attendance under penalty.
Doctrinal statement of the Church of England, finalised in 1571, defining its Protestant theology.
Catholic heir presumptive imprisoned in England 1568-87; executed at Fotheringhay on 8 February 1587 after the Babington Plot.
Catholic conspiracy to assassinate Elizabeth and free Mary, exposed by Walsingham's intelligence network.
Fleet of 130 ships sent by Philip II in summer 1588, defeated in the Channel (Gravelines, 8 August) and wrecked off Scotland and Ireland.

walkthroughs.body_html: Elizabeth accepted the title Supreme Governor (not Head, easing Catholic and female-rule scruples). The Act of Uniformity (1559) imposed the 1559 Prayer Book, splitting the difference between 1549 and 1552; the Royal Injunctions (1559) regulated worship. The Settlement frustrated both Puritans (Vestments Controversy from 1566; Admonition to the Parliament 1572) and Catholics.

Mary Stuart fled to England in 1568. The Northern Rebellion (1569) and Ridolfi Plot (1571) circled around her. The papal bull Regnans in Excelsis (1570) excommunicated Elizabeth. The Throckmorton Plot (1583) and especially the Babington Plot (1586) implicated Mary; Walsingham produced the incriminating evidence. Mary was executed at Fotheringhay on 8 February 1587.

Philip II's 'Enterprise of England' launched in May 1588 under Medina Sidonia. After skirmishes up the Channel, English fireships at Calais (night of 7 August) broke the crescent formation, and at Gravelines (8 August) superior English gunnery prevailed. Storms scattered the fleet around Scotland and Ireland; perhaps 60 ships and over 10,000 men were lost. War with Spain dragged on until 1604.
